title: Review: Current, potential difference and resistance; Series and parallel circuits

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Resistance
items.clue: The opposition of a component to the flow of charge.

items.label: Series connection
items.clue: Components joined one after another in a single loop.

items.label: Junction
items.clue: A point where the conducting path divides or rejoins.

items.label: Light-dependent resistor (LDR)
items.clue: Conducts better in bright conditions than in the dark; used as a sensor.

questions.stem: In the resistance practical, why is the voltmeter connected across the test wire rather than in the loop with it?

options.text: because a voltmeter in the loop would read the current in it instead
because it must compare the potentials at the two ends of the wire
because a voltmeter, like the ammeter, belongs in the loop
because pd flows through it, so the voltmeter sits in the loop

questions.explanation: Potential difference is a difference between two points, so the meter must be connected to both ends of the component — across it.

questions.stem: The light shining on an LDR is made brighter. What happens to the resistance of the LDR?

options.text: it decreases as the light on it gets brighter
it increases, as there is more light for it to resist
it stays constant whatever the light level may be
it rises steadily as the light on it grows brighter

questions.explanation: The resistance of an LDR decreases as light intensity increases, from millions of ohms in the dark to a few hundred in bright light.

questions.stem: A 9 V supply is connected in series with a 2 Ω resistor and a 4 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across the 4 Ω resistor?

options.text: 9 V, as each component has the whole supply across it
4.5 V, as the supply is shared equally between them
6 V, from the 1.5 A current in the 4 Ω resistor
3 V, an equal share among the three parts

questions.explanation: Total resistance 6 Ω gives a current of 1.5 A, and 1.5 A × 4 Ω = 6 V across the larger resistor.

questions.stem: A current of 0.50 A passes through a 12 Ω resistor. Calculate the potential difference across the resistor.
questions.explanation: V = I R = 0.50 × 12 = 6.0 V, with potential difference in volts, V.

questions.stem: An LDR is part of a circuit that switches a street lamp on when it gets dark. What happens as darkness falls?

options.text: the LDR's resistance falls, so a bigger current can switch the lamp on
the LDR's resistance rises, and so the circuit switches the lamp on
the LDR's resistance falls, so the lamp is kept switched off
the LDR's resistance does not change, but the pd across it falls

questions.explanation: Less light means a higher LDR resistance, and the switching circuit responds to that change by turning the street lamp on.

questions.stem: Three 6 Ω resistors are connected in series across a 9 V supply. Using the idea of equivalent resistance, what current does the supply deliver?

options.text: 1.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of 6 Ω alone
0.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of 18 Ω
3 A, using an equivalent resistance of just 3 Ω
4.5 A, using an equivalent resistance of just 2 Ω

questions.explanation: The three series resistances add to an equivalent 18 Ω, and 9 V ÷ 18 Ω = 0.5 A.

questions.stem: A 3.0 Ω resistor and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in series. What is the total resistance of the combination?

options.text: it is 2.0 Ω, because the charge now divides between two paths
it is 9.0 Ω, because series resistances add together
it is 6.0 Ω, set by the larger of the two resistors
it is 4.5 Ω, the average of the two resistance values

questions.explanation: Resistors in series are joined end to end, so the charge passes through both and their resistances add: 3.0 Ω + 6.0 Ω = 9.0 Ω, which is larger than either resistor alone.

questions.stem: Which circuit would let a student measure the resistance of a fixed resistor?

options.text: a voltmeter in the loop with an ammeter across the resistor
an ammeter and a voltmeter both in the loop with the resistor
an ammeter in the loop and a voltmeter across the resistor
a voltmeter across the cell with an ammeter across the resistor

questions.explanation: The ammeter gives the current through the component and the voltmeter the pd across it, so R = V ÷ I can be calculated.

questions.stem: In a circuit a cell is joined to a resistor, and the resistor is joined to two lamps that are placed side by side between the same pair of junctions. How is this circuit best described?

options.text: It has both kinds of part: the resistor is in series with a parallel pair of lamps
It is a series circuit, because all of the components are joined to one cell
It is a parallel circuit, because the circuit contains more than one branch
It is neither, because a circuit has to be all series or all parallel

questions.explanation: Some circuits include both series and parallel parts, and this is one of them.

questions.stem: A student plots I–V graphs for a fixed resistor at constant temperature and for a filament lamp. What do the two shapes tell her?

options.text: the resistor has the greater resistance, because its line is the steeper
both elements are linear, because in each of them the current rises as the pd rises
the lamp is linear with constant R, while the resistor's R falls as the current rises
the resistor is a linear element of constant R, while the lamp is non-linear and its R rises

questions.stem: Three lamps are connected in series with a cell. One lamp is taken out of its holder. What happens to the other two lamps?

options.text: They both stay lit, because each lamp has its own path back to the cell
They both stay lit but shine brighter, as the total resistance falls
They both go out, because the single path round the circuit has been broken
The lamp before the empty holder stays lit, but the lamp after it goes out

questions.explanation: In series there is only one path, so removing any component stops the current everywhere in the loop.

questions.stem: In Required practical activity 4 the resistor must be kept at a constant temperature. Why does this matter?

options.text: so that any change of resistance from heating cannot spoil the results
so that the resistor does not become hot enough to be dangerous to touch
so that the cell is not drained by the current passing through the wire
so that the ammeter and voltmeter readings are taken at the same time

questions.explanation: The point of the investigation is the resistor's ohmic behaviour, which appears only if its temperature, and so its resistance, is held steady.
